marks: The Early Slavs, who lived across central, eastern and southeastern Europe from the 5th century, shared almost the same words for religious ideas.
Vladimir raised idols of Perun, Dazhbog, Stribog, Simargl and Mokosh on a hill here in 980; after his baptism in 988 they were burned or thrown into the Dnieper.
Adam of Bremen described the Triglav of Wolin as “Neptune of the three natures”.
The temple-stronghold of the four-headed Svetovid on Rugia surrendered to King Valdemar I of Denmark in 1168, and Bishop Absalon destroyed the temple.
A holy place of the old faith at Kobarid, in present-day Slovenia, was stamped out in a “crusade” in 1331.
notes: The Early Slavs live across central, eastern and southeastern Europe; Procopius (6th century) writes that they hold the god of lightning to be lord over all and sacrifice bulls to him.
The South Slavs settle in Southeastern Europe and come into contact with Christianity under the emperor Heraclius (610–641).
Great Moravia (863) and Bulgaria (864) adopt Christianity, after Cyril and Methodius create the first Slavic script (855); the Bohemian dukes had accepted it in 845.
Mieszko I of Poland is baptised (966); Vladimir sets up a pantheon of Slavic gods at Kiev (980), then is baptised (988) and has the idols destroyed.
An uprising against Christianity breaks out among the West Slavs in the 1030s, rebellions follow among Poles and East Slavs through the 11th century, and volkhvs lead revolts in Rus’.
The Northern Crusades impose Catholicism on the Baltic West Slavs; Arkona falls to the Danes in 1168 and the temple of Svetovid is destroyed.
A holy place of the old faith at Kobarid is stamped out (1331); the old gods live on in folk religion and the “double faith”.
src: Helmold of Bosau, Chronica Slavorum (12th century)
